clue.text: Dawdle round smallest room, going back for potty

indicators.note: to go round something is to enclose it, so the dawdling word wraps the toilet word

parts.note: to dally is to dawdle or linger

indicators.note: going back means travelling in the opposite direction, so the toilet word is read right to left

parts.note: the smallest room is a jokey name for the toilet, the loo

explanation.surface: Someone loafing about the toilet and then going back for a child's potty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Potty' looks like the child's pot, but it is the adjective meaning mad. DOOLALLY is British slang for crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are informal British slang for being slightly mad or crazy.

clue.text: Place is turned upside down having broken in to warehouse

indicators.note: breaking into a building means getting inside it

parts.note: a depot is a storehouse

indicators.note: in a down clue, upside down means the word reads from bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A burglary leaves a warehouse turned upside down.
explanation.definitionFit: To deposit something is to put or set it down somewhere, so it is a verb synonym.

clue.text: Topless broadcast, private

indicators.note: topless means losing the top, which in a down answer is the first letter

parts.note: seed broadcast is scattered, that is sown

explanation.surface: A topless show is aired on television, though meant to be private.
explanation.definitionFit: Something one's own is personal, belonging only to oneself rather than shared.

clue.text: Pudding to eat that's smelly?

parts.note: afters is British slang for pudding, the course after the main
to have a meal is to eat it

explanation.surface: A dessert that smells a little off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smelly' sounds like an insult, but the question mark softens it: the answer is something with a scent.
explanation.definitionFit: Aftershave is a scented lotion, so it is something that deliberately gives off a smell.

clue.text: Switch over everything that's plain

indicators.note: to switch is to swap around, so the joined words are turned end to end

parts.note: over in the sense of on top of
all is everything

explanation.surface: Turning everything over to make it plain.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'over' puts its word above the next, giving ONALL to be switched.
explanation.definitionFit: A llano is a treeless grassy plain of South America, the Spanish term for flat lowland.

clue.text: Muslim greeting mother, unfortunately rejected

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so these words are read in the opposite direction

parts.note: an informal word for mother
an exclamation of regret, said when something goes badly

explanation.surface: Someone greets their mother in the Muslim way and is sadly rebuffed.
explanation.definitionFit: Salaam, Arabic for peace, is the customary greeting used among Muslims.

clue.text: A river? No — and yes!

parts.note: taken as written
R is the map abbreviation for river
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether it is a river, and is told no, and then yes.
explanation.walkthrough: The first three words build the letters; 'and yes!' then confirms that the result really is a river.
explanation.definitionFit: The Arno is the river that flows through Florence and Pisa in Tuscany.

clue.text: Misplace a Cornishman such as Trevithick going via Eurostar?

definitions.text: Misplace a Cornishman such as Trevithick going via Eurostar?

indicators.note: to misplace is to put in the wrong spot, so the letters are put in a new order

parts.note: the two words taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A Cornish railway pioneer imagined travelling on the Channel Tunnel train.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition as well: misplacing an old Cornish engineer in time is the very thing the answer names. Richard Trevithick built early steam locomotives around 1800.
explanation.definitionFit: An anachronism is something placed in the wrong period of time, like an 1800s engineer on a modern train.

clue.text: Clear a path for a garden centre in spring

indicators.note: to centre something in another word is to set it in the middle of it

parts.note: May is a spring month
taken as written
Kew Gardens is the botanic garden in west London

explanation.surface: Clearing a path for a garden centre opening in spring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Garden centre' reads as a shop selling plants, but 'centre' is the instruction to put A and KEW in the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: To make way is to step aside or clear room so that something can pass through.

clue.text: If end is nigh, ultimately it's destroyed?

definitions.text: If end is nigh, ultimately it's destroyed?

indicators.note: something destroyed is broken apart, so its letters are scattered and rebuilt

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: ultimately points to the very last letter of the word before it

parts.note: the final letter of nigh

explanation.surface: A prophet of doom warns that if the end is near, everything will be wiped out.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: something destroyed when the end is nigh is done for.
explanation.definitionFit: Finished can mean ruined or done for, which is what something destroyed at the end would be.

clue.text: Slash, say, ludicrous amount, in cut that's put in place

indicators.note: something ludicrous is absurd and out of order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written
to park something is to put it in place and leave it there

explanation.surface: A huge, silly sum of money is slashed from a budget once the cut is put in place.
explanation.walkthrough: A composite anagram: the fodder is AMOUNT, IN and CUT plus PARK, a word supplied for 'put in place', all shuffled together into PUNCTUATION MARK.
explanation.definitionFit: The slash, or oblique stroke, is one example of a symbol used in writing to separate or punctuate.

clue.text: Posh type feeding so very fast

indicators.note: food goes into a mouth, so feeding here means going inside the next word

parts.note: Latin for 'so' or 'thus', used to mark a quotation as printed
U means upper-class, as in U and non-U
a type of person is simply a person

explanation.surface: An upper-class sort eats so very quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: A U person is an upper-class one, from the U and non-U debate on posh English. SIC is the Latin 'so' editors print after a quoted slip.
explanation.definitionFit: Supersonic speed exceeds the speed of sound, which is about as fast as ordinary travel gets.

clue.text: Subject of a parable supporting love and redemption, ultimately

definitions.text: Subject of a parable supporting love and redemption, ultimately

parts.note: surface reading: the central figure of one of the Gospel parables
setter's reading: the story of the wasteful young man who squanders his inheritance and is ultimately welcomed home with love and forgiveness

explanation.walkthrough: In Luke's Gospel a younger son wastes his inheritance, returns in shame and is welcomed back by his father, a story of love and redemption.
explanation.definitionFit: The returning spendthrift is the central character of the best-known parable about forgiveness.

clue.text: I'm baking first of pastries, then having chop

indicators.note: first of asks for only the opening letter of the following word

parts.note: the opening letter of pastries
to hew is to chop, as with an axe

explanation.surface: A baker sets to work on pastries and then has a chop for lunch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I'm baking' sounds like someone at the oven, but it means 'I'm boiling hot'.
explanation.definitionFit: Phew is the exclamation of someone sweltering, the same complaint as saying they are roasting hot.

clue.text: Gutless individual pinning stigma on passionate author

indicators.note: to pin something is to hold it fast between, so the outer letters grip the rest
gutless means with the insides removed, leaving only the outer letters

parts.note: one is a single individual
a scar is a lasting mark, a stigma
wild means unrestrained and passionate

explanation.surface: A spineless person brands a passionate writer with shame.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' means sitting above, so the stigma comes before the passion, and both are held by what is left of a gutted individual.
explanation.definitionFit: Oscar Wilde was an Irish playwright and novelist, so he is an example of a writer.

clue.text: Darts mark in wood, not quite a foot

indicators.note: in places the darts word inside the timber word

parts.note: a tree is a wood-producing plant, and wood here stands for it

indicators.note: not quite means falling a little short, so the final letter is lost

parts.note: the oche is the line a darts player stands behind

explanation.surface: A darts player's throwing line is chalked on a wooden floor, a little under twelve inches away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Foot' is the unit of verse, not of length. The darts line sits inside the plant, and 'not quite' trims the extra final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A trochee is a metrical foot of one stressed syllable followed by an unstressed one.

clue.text: The last bit noted, nip off

indicators.note: off suggests something gone bad or awry, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Somebody noted the final part and then nipped off.
explanation.definitionFit: An endpoint is the final stage or terminal of something, the place where it stops.

clue.text: Man's right — it's all happened

parts.note: belonging to a man is his
a Tory is a member of the UK Conservative party, on the political right

explanation.surface: A man declares he was right all along, since it has all come to pass.
explanation.definitionFit: History is the record of past events, everything that has already taken place.

clue.text: Girl filling in crossword was suffering

indicators.note: a filling sits inside something, so the girl goes into the middle

parts.note: a crossword is set out in a grid
Eve is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A girl filling in a crossword was having a hard time of it.
explanation.definitionFit: To have grieved is to have felt deep sorrow, a past form of suffering.

clue.text: Stomach taking a moment to contract, wind first

indicators.note: to contract is to shrink, so the moment word loses its final letter
first tells the solver the wind word goes at the front of the answer

parts.note: wind is gas in the gut
a trice is a moment, as in 'in a trice'

explanation.surface: A stomach cramps for a moment, the wind going first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stomach' looks like a noun, but here it is used as a modifier, as in stomach pains, and so means gastric.
explanation.definitionFit: Gastric is the adjective for anything relating to the stomach, as in gastric juices.

clue.text: Frank, say, needs help to roll joint, wife having left

indicators.note: a thing that rolls over turns end to end, so the help word is turned around

parts.note: aid is help

indicators.note: the wife having left means her letter departs from the joint word

parts.note: the wrist is a joint of the arm
W is the standard abbreviation for wife

explanation.surface: Frank needs a hand rolling a joint now his wife has gone.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests cannabis, but the joint is the wrist. Frank is Anne Frank, whose wartime diary made her famous.
explanation.definitionFit: Anne Frank is the best-known example of a diary writer, so she stands for the general class.

clue.text: Touching line, chap's a shade above it

parts.note: tan is a light brown shade
a gent is a chap; the 's is the verb 'is'

explanation.surface: A man standing by the touchline whose skin is a shade darker.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, TAN sitting above GENT means TAN comes first. 'Touching line' looks like the rugby or football touchline.
explanation.definitionFit: In geometry a tangent is a straight line that meets a curve at one point without crossing it.

clue.text: One away from land, finds bridge

indicators.note: one taken away from the land word leaves it a letter shorter

parts.note: a land, that is a country
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A traveller far from home comes across a bridge.
explanation.definitionFit: A span is the stretch of a bridge between supports, and as a verb to span is to bridge.

clue.text: Groom who's on mare — or bride on stallion, possibly?

indicators.note: in an across clue, one thing on another is written after it, so the bride follows the stallion

parts.note: a stallion is a male horse
a bride is a woman on her wedding day

explanation.surface: A wedding couple riding off, the groom on a mare and the bride on a stallion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Groom' looks like the bridegroom, but it is a stable hand who rides; 'possibly' admits that such a groom need not be female.
explanation.definitionFit: A horsewoman is a female rider, and a groom mounted on a mare could be one.

clue.text: Ancient club just around the corner welcoming pensioners, primarily

indicators.note: to welcome someone is to take them in, so the time word holds the letter

parts.note: something just around the corner will happen soon

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so only the opening letter is used

parts.note: the opening letter of pensioners

explanation.surface: An old social club nearby takes in senior citizens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Club' suggests a society, but it is a golf club: the spoon was an old wooden club, roughly a modern three-wood.
explanation.definitionFit: The spoon is an obsolete golf club, so an ancient club in the sporting sense.

clue.text: Native of Espoo punching elf in Norway

indicators.note: a punch goes into its target, so the answer is driven into the run of words

parts.note: the letters run across the three words, from the end of the first into the last

explanation.surface: A man from Espoo throws a punch at a Norwegian elf.
explanation.walkthrough: Espoo is a city in Finland, next to Helsinki.
explanation.definitionFit: A Finn is a person from Finland, the country where Espoo lies.

clue.text: A lottery never lost twice?

parts.note: surface reading: a raffle or prize draw that nobody ever loses
setter's reading: a deadly game of chance where whoever loses once dies, so cannot lose again

explanation.walkthrough: In this game a revolver with one bullet is spun and fired at one's own head; the loser does not get a second go.
explanation.definitionFit: This lethal gamble is a pure game of chance, so calling it a lottery is grimly accurate.

clue.text: Heavyweight down then?

parts.note: surface reading: a big boxer who has been knocked to the canvas
setter's reading: a large unit of weight, entered down the grid; read upwards it spells the word for a negative

explanation.surface: A heavyweight boxer, floored, and the question of what next.
explanation.walkthrough: A guess at the setter's joke: the weight sits in a down light, and read the other way, upwards, it gives a word for no.
explanation.definitionFit: A ton is a large unit of mass, roughly a thousand kilograms, so it is a heavy weight.

clue.text: Third of incisors, a square tooth

indicators.note: third of asks for the letter in third position of the following word

parts.note: the third letter of incisors
taken as written
nine is a square number, three times three

explanation.surface: A dentist counts teeth: a third of the incisors and a square-edged tooth.
explanation.definitionFit: A canine is the pointed tooth beside the incisors, so it is one specific tooth.

clue.text: Means of communication in flier — and requiring translation

indicators.note: requiring translation says the word 'and' must be put into a foreign language first

parts.note: taken as written
a tern is a seabird, so a flier
et is French for and

explanation.surface: A message delivered by a flying bird or plane needs to be translated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flier' suggests a pilot or a leaflet, but it is a bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The internet is a global network carrying email and messages, a modern channel for people to communicate.
